newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU farmers' new Finnish boss stresses food safety.
newsitem.headline: EU farmers' new Finnish boss stresses food safety.

text.p: European Union farmers need to work closely with consumers and industry to guarantee food safety, Risto Volanen, the new manager of the powerful EU farmers' and farm cooperative lobbies COPA, said on Wednesday.
"I would like to see closer cooperation between all people in the food chain from the farm to industry to the kitchen table," Volanen, a 52-year-old Finn, told Reuters.

In his first interview with an international agency since taking office in early March, Volanen, a former deputy director general of a Finnish farm cooperative, said that farmers wanted to be good partners on fair terms.
"In the food sector we depend on each other. It's in the common interest of farmers and consumers that there is a well run (food) system to provide confidence," he stressed.
Asked about the impact of the massive public health scare over mad cow disease, or bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), Volanen said cautiously that it had helped change attitudes.
"Before, development was a question of quantity and price. The table is now turning towards a recognition of common interest in good quality food," he said.
Volanen was unanimously appointed after being the only candidate for one of the most difficult jobs in European agriculture - representing eight million farms and more than 30,000 farm cooperatives.
The post, was vacant for one year after the previous French incumbent left prematurely after only two years.
"It's a very hard job," Volanen said, referring to the task of welding 15 highly diverse national farming industries into a united and effective lobbying force.
Variations between EU countries and products would increase as the EU enlarged eastwards, he added.
Coming from Finland, where agriculture is tiny when compared with the rest of Europe, he admitted he faced a huge task.
"The job is 100 percent more than in Finland," he said.
Asked about the threat of new farm price and subsidy cuts, he said that reform was nothing new, adding that in a changing environment there is continuous change.
Spending should also be put in perspective, he added. The 40 billion Ecus ($45 billion) farm budget absorbed around 50 percent of the EU budget but amounted to only about 0.5 percent of EU GNP.
The founding fathers decided that agriculture should be a basic building block of the Community, he said, adding that it was still the most "europeanised" policy.
COPA, which was born with and grew up with the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), has coped with tremendous change, he pointed out.
In the early 1950s some 30 percent of the European workforce was in agriculture but this had now fallen to five percent and to only two percent in the most industrialised countries, he noted.
But farmers needed to find effective ways to meet budgetary pressures, a new round of world farm subsidy cutting talks and EU expansion eastwards, he said.
"The train is moving quite fast" he said. "European farmers increasingly need a strong and united organisation to deal with the new challenges."
